a: most excellent Diognetus
p: A man of rank, addressed with a title. Who he was is unknown.
b: The title kratiste, 'most excellent', is the one Luke gives Theophilus (Luke 1:3) and that letters and speakers in Acts give the governors Felix and Festus (Acts 23:26; Acts 24:3; Acts 26:25): a courtesy for a man of standing. Lake: 'The Diognetus to whom it is addressed is unknown, though some scholars have sought to identify him with a Diognetus who was a teacher of Marcus Aurelius.' The Catholic Encyclopedia (J. Chapman, 1909) judges that identification 'at most plausible'. Lake also doubts whether the work was 'an actual apology sent to a living person' at all, or 'an academic treatise or possibly the exercise of some young theologian'.

a: reverence for God
t: Reverence for God: the writer's word for the faith
p: Greek theosebeia, 'reverence for God', the writer's name for the Christian religion.
b: The writer calls Christianity theosebeia, 'reverence for God' or 'God-fearing' (1:1; 4:5-6; 6:4), and uses the verb at 3:1. The site keeps it apart from eusebeia, 'godliness' (1 Timothy 3:16), so the reader can see which word stands where. The same word appears once in the New Testament, at 1 Timothy 2:10, where the site has 'women who say they honor God'. It was a word an educated pagan would respect: the writer presents the faith as true piety, set against the Greeks' folly (2) and what he calls the Jews' superstition (1:1; 4:1).

a: think nothing of death
t: Christians who did not fear death
p: Outsiders noticed that Christians were ready to die. The writer comes back to it at 7:7-9 and 10:7-8.
b: Diognetus's first question is what kind of God makes people 'look down on the world and think nothing of death'. The answer comes in pieces: Christians are only resident aliens in the world (5:5; 6:8); they are thrown to wild beasts and are not overcome (7:7-8); and once a person knows the real death and 'that other fire', the short fire of the martyrs seems small (10:7-8). The Martyrdom of Polycarp says the same of its martyrs, who 'looked down on the tortures of this world' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 2:3).

a: the superstition of the Jews
p: Greek deisidaimonia, fear of the gods carried too far. Here plainly a put-down.
b: Deisidaimonia is literally 'fear of divine powers'. It could be neutral: Festus uses it of the Jews' 'religion' in Acts 25:19, and Paul tells the Athenians they are 'very devoted to the gods' (Acts 17:22, the adjective). Here, as again at 4:1 ('their superstition about the Sabbath'), it is a sneer: religion as anxious, needless fear. The writer's whole account of Judaism (3-4) should be read with this word in mind; see the note at 4:1.

a: deep affection
p: Greek philostorgia, the warm love of parents and children, used of Christians for each other.
b: Philostorgia is the natural love within a family. Paul uses the adjective in Romans 12:10, which the site renders 'Be devoted to one another with the love of a family'. Diognetus has noticed that Christians treat one another as kin. The writer never answers this question head on, but 5:6-7, 5:11 and 10:4-6 show the love he means.

a: this new race
p: Greek genos, 'race, kind, people'. Diognetus sees Christians as a new kind of people.
b: Genos means a people of common descent or a kind; epitēdeuma, the word joined to it, is a practice or way of life. The question treats Christians as a new group in the world, neither Greek nor Jew. Aristides' Apology, which Lake names as the closest likeness to this letter, says there are 'four classes of men in this world:— Barbarians and Greeks, Jews and Christians' (Apology 2, in the English of the Ante-Nicene Fathers). The site's 1 Peter 2:9 calls the church 'a chosen family' (Greek genos), and the Martyrdom of Polycarp speaks of 'the God-loving and God-fearing race of the Christians' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 3:2). The writer's answer (5:1-5) is that Christians are not set apart by land, speech or customs at all.

a: now, and not earlier
p: A standard objection: if Christianity is true, why is it new? The writer answers in 8-9.
b: Ancient people trusted what was old; a new religion looked suspect. Diognetus asks why this way of life came 'now, and not earlier'. The writer answers at length: God kept his plan hidden in a mystery and seemed not to care (8:10); he let people show that they could not reach life on their own; then 'the time came' to show his kindness (9:1-2). The New Testament makes a like point: 'when the time had come to its fullness, God sent out his Son' (Galatians 4:4). The homily of chapter 11 answers the same charge another way: the Word 'appeared as new' but 'was discovered to be old' (11:4).

a: a new human being
p: The writer asks Diognetus to start fresh, in words that recall Paul's 'new self'.
b: 'Become like a new human being (kainos anthrōpos) from the very start.' Paul uses the same words for the life a believer puts on: 'put on the new self, created in line with God' (Ephesians 4:24). Here it is the beginning of a hearing, not yet conversion: the inquirer must set aside the customs he grew up with before he can judge the case.

a: a new word
p: Greek logos: a message, an account, and the name the writer gives the Son (7:2).
b: Logos can mean a word, a message, an argument or reason. The writer will use it for the one God sent, 'the holy Word' (7:2). Keeping 'word' here lets the reader hear the link: Diognetus is about to hear a new logos, and the subject of it is the Logos himself.

a: like the stone people walk on
t: Gods of stone, bronze and clay
p: The mockery of idols follows the Hebrew prophets and psalms.
b: The list of materials, and the point that a god is only the stuff a craftsman worked, is the argument of Isaiah 44:9-20 (the carpenter who burns half a log and bows to the rest), Jeremiah 10:3-5 and Psalm 115:4-8. The Wisdom of Solomon, a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, says the same: 'miserable are those who set their hopes on dead things' (Wisdom of Solomon 13:10). The writer adds a Greek touch of his own: the stone of a god is no better than the paving stone underfoot.
r: Isaiah 44:9-20; Jeremiah 10:3-5; Psalm 115:4-8; Wisdom of Solomon 13:10; Deuteronomy 4:28

a: open to being made over into something else
p: The Greek here lacks a main verb. Lake's note gives the sense.
b: The clause runs, word for word, 'before by their crafts into the shape of these to be stamped, which each of them for each, still even now, transformed?' The grammar is incomplete, and the Plain English Translation gives the sense. Lake's note: 'The meaning is that, given the requisite workers, the material used for ordinary vessels of wood or brass or silver might at any moment be turned into a ‘god.’' In other words, the god and the kitchen pot are the same kind of thing, and the difference is only which craftsman got hold of the metal.

a: Are they not all mute?
p: The string of questions echoes Psalm 115.
b: Psalm 115 says of idols: 'A mouth they have, but they cannot speak' (Psalm 115:5), and it goes through eyes, ears, nose, hands and feet. Psalm 135:15-18 repeats it, and Habakkuk mocks the one who says 'to a silent stone, "Rouse yourself!"' (Habakkuk 2:19). The Greek kōphos can mean either 'mute' or 'deaf'; the writer uses it again at 3:3 and 3:5, where the site has 'cannot hear' and 'deaf'.

a: you end up becoming just like them
p: The psalm's warning, in a single phrase.
b: 'The ones who make them will end up like them, / everyone who trusts in them' (Psalm 115:8). The writer gives the warning in the second person: you who worship things without sense become senseless yourselves.

a: So you hate Christians for this
p: Christians were disliked for not honoring the city's gods.
b: The writer suggests that the hatred Diognetus has noticed comes from the Christians' refusal to treat images as gods. In the Martyrdom of Polycarp the crowd shouts 'Away with the atheists!' for the same reason. The letter returns to the hatred at 5:11-17 and 6:5: those who hate Christians 'cannot say why'. Jesus had said, 'If the world hates you, remember: it has hated me ahead of you' (John 15:18).

a: post guards beside them by day
p: A god that must be guarded from thieves cannot guard anyone.
b: The gold and silver images were locked up and watched; the cheap ones were left out. The writer's point is that the worshipers themselves show what they think of their gods: they treat them as property. Jeremiah mocked idols in a like way: 'Someone always has to pick them up, for they take no steps' (Jeremiah 10:5).

a: the smoke of burning fat
t: Blood and the smoke of fat
p: Greek knisa, the savory smoke from an altar. The writer uses the same pair for the Jewish sacrifices (3:5).
b: Knisa is the smell and smoke of fat roasting on an altar, the part of a sacrifice that went up to the gods in Greek worship. 'Blood and the smoke of fat' here, of the Greeks, is repeated word for word at 3:5, of the Jewish sacrifices. The repetition is deliberate: the writer will argue that the two kinds of offering are alike.

a: this punishment
p: Greek kolasis. The writer uses it in irony here, and of God's punishment at 9:2 and 10:7.
b: Kolasis is the site's 'punishment' throughout this book. The writer's joke is that the 'honors' paid to idols, being hacked, smeared with blood and smoked, would be torture to anyone who could feel. The same word is serious later: our wrongdoing's 'wages, punishment and death' (9:2) and the eternal fire that 'will punish to the end' (10:7).

a: revere God in the same way as the Jews
t: Why not worship as the Jews do?
p: Chapters 3-4 give the writer's case against Jewish worship. Lake: like most early apologies.
b: Lake describes the plan: 'Like most early apologies for Christianity it begins by expounding the foolishness of the worship of idols, and the inadequacy of the Jewish religion'. The writer grants the Jews more than the Greeks (3:2) but then treats their sacrifices as no better than offerings to idols (3:3-5) and their observances as 'laughable' (4:1). How readers today weigh these chapters is in the note at 4:1.

a: honor one God of all things and think of him as Master
t: The Jews worship the one God
p: The writer grants that the Jews rightly worship one God, the Master of all.
b: Insofar as they keep away from idols, the Jews are right to claim one God of all things: the confession of Deuteronomy 6:4, 'Listen, Israel: The LORD is our God. The LORD is one.' Despotēs, 'Master', is the word the site uses for God in Luke 2:29 and Acts 4:24. The writer's complaint is not about which God the Jews worship but about how: with offerings, as if God needed them.

a: as if he needed them
p: An old argument, from the Psalms and Paul at Athens.
b: Psalm 50 has God say, 'Do I feed on the flesh of strong bulls? / Do I drink goats' blood?' (Psalm 50:13). Paul told the Athenians that God is not served by human hands 'as if he were short of anything' (Acts 17:25). Justin Martyr made the same point to the emperor: 'God does not need the material offerings which men can give' (First Apology 10, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers). The writer turns the argument, which the Bible aims at sacrifice without obedience, against sacrifice itself.

a: he who made heaven and earth and all that is in them
p: Lake's margin: Exodus 20:11, Psalm 146:6 and Acts 14:15.
b: The phrase is the Bible's way of naming God as Creator: in the Sabbath commandment (Exodus 20:11), in the psalms (Psalm 146:6) and in the prayer of the Jerusalem church (Acts 4:24) and in Paul's speech at Lystra, the God 'who made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them' (Acts 14:15). The writer leaves out 'the sea'. At Lystra, too, the point was spoken against sacrifice: the crowd was about to offer bulls to Paul and Barnabas (Acts 14:13).

a: no different from those who show the same eagerness toward deaf idols
p: The writer goes further than the prophets: he treats the sacrifices themselves as folly.
b: Where it matches: the prophets warned that sacrifice without justice is worthless (Isaiah 1:11-17; Hosea 6:6; Psalm 50:8-15), and Hebrews says that 'the law holds a shadow of the good things to come' and that its sacrifices 'can never make perfect' (Hebrews 10:1), now that Christ has been offered. Where it conflicts: in the Law, God himself commands the offerings (Leviticus 1:1-2) and accepts them as 'a soothing smell' (Leviticus 1:9). The writer never says that God gave these laws; he sets the temple offerings beside offerings to deaf idols, which neither the prophets nor Hebrews do.

a: jumpy fear about foods
p: Greek psophodees, 'scared of every sound', like a skittish horse.
b: The adjective is built from psophos, 'a noise', and deos, 'fear': timid, startled at any sound. The writer pictures the food laws as nervousness. Eirōneia, 'pretense', later in the verse, is the word behind English 'irony': saying one thing and meaning another, a show.

a: these things are laughable and not worth a word
t: Read beside the Bible, and what the Catholic Church teaches today
p: The writer mocks the food laws, Sabbath, circumcision and feasts. The Bible itself says they were God's gift to Israel.
b: The writer calls the Jewish observances 'laughable' and their keepers boastful (4:1, 4:6), and he never says that God gave them. Read beside the Bible, three things stand out. First, the Law presents these practices as God's own commands to Israel (Genesis 17:10-14; Exodus 20:8-11; Leviticus 11), and Paul lists 'the covenants, and the lawgiving, and the sacred service' among Israel's gifts (Romans 9:4). Second, the New Testament does say that Gentile Christians are not bound by them (Galatians 4:10; Colossians 2:16; Mark 7:19), so the writer's conclusion that Christians need not keep them has New Testament roots, though his scorn does not. Third, this kind of language fed the long history of Christian contempt for Jews that the site's anti-Judaism page traces. The Catholic Church's Second Vatican Council taught that 'the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God' and that the Church 'decries hatred, persecutions, displays of anti-Semitism, directed against Jews at any time and by anyone' (Nostra Aetate 4). The text is translated as it stands; it is not softened.

a: how is that not unlawful?
t: Compared with the Bible: clean and unclean food
p: The writer's argument is close to 1 Timothy 4, but turned against the food laws of Moses.
b: Matches: the New Testament teaches that 'Every created thing God made is good. None of it should be thrown out when it is taken with thanks' (1 Timothy 4:4), and Mark reports that Jesus 'made all foods clean' (Mark 7:19). Goes beyond: 1 Timothy aims at teachers who 'tell them to keep clear of foods' (1 Timothy 4:3), not at Israel's law; Leviticus 11 presents the distinction of clean and unclean as God's command to Israel, and the writer calls keeping it 'lawless'. The irony of the word is his: to obey the Law is called breaking what is right.

a: as if he forbade doing any good thing on the Sabbath day
p: The writer uses the Gospels' Sabbath debates as a charge against all Jews.
b: In the Gospels Jesus asks, 'Is it allowed on the Sabbath to do something good, or something bad?' (Mark 3:4), and concludes, 'So doing good on the Sabbath is allowed' (Matthew 12:12). Those were arguments among Jews about how to keep the day, which Jesus himself kept. The writer turns them into an accusation that the Jews slander God, and he does not ask, as the Gospels do, what the Sabbath is for (Mark 2:27). The site's cards at Exodus 20 and Matthew 12 give how the churches answer whether Christians must keep the Sabbath.

a: the cutting short of the flesh
p: A scornful phrase for circumcision, like Paul's 'mutilation' in Philippians 3:2.
b: Meiōsis tēs sarkos is literally 'a lessening of the flesh'. Paul, in a hot moment, called those who demanded circumcision of Gentiles 'the mutilation' (Philippians 3:2), and he taught that 'circumcision is of the heart' (Romans 2:29). But Paul never mocked circumcision as Israel's sign of God's covenant (Genesis 17:10-11; Romans 4:11). The writer denies that it is a 'proof that they are chosen', where Genesis calls it 'the sign of the covenant'.

a: keep close watch on the stars and the moon
p: The Jewish year runs by the moon. The writer calls the careful reckoning folly.
b: Israel's months began with the new moon, and its feasts and fasts fell on fixed days of the moon's months (Numbers 28:11-14; Leviticus 23). The writer pictures Jews 'sitting beside' the stars and moon to divide God's seasons into feasts and mourning. Paul had warned Gentile believers against 'keeping close track of days, months, seasons and years' (Galatians 4:10). In 7:2 the same writer praises the moon that 'obeys' the Word: the heavens are God's to rule, not ours to watch for set days.

a: God's plans
p: Greek oikonomia, 'household management', the writer's word for God's ordering of things (7:1; 9:1).
b: Oikonomia is the running of a household; in the New Testament, God's plan (Ephesians 1:10; Ephesians 3:9) or a steward's task (1 Corinthians 9:17). The site renders it 'plan'. Here the plural means God's ordering of the seasons; at 7:1 the word comes back, and at 9:1 the verb ('he had already planned everything').

a: the mystery of their own reverence for God
p: Greek mystērion: not a puzzle but a secret of God, now made known.
b: The writer ends his attack on Greeks and Jews by saying that the Christians' own faith cannot be learned 'from a human being'. A mystērion in the New Testament is something hidden that God has made known (Romans 16:25; Colossians 1:26). The next chapters explain it: God himself sent his Word (7:1-2) and revealed his plan through his servant (8:9-11).

a: it is not by land, speech or customs that Christians differ
p: Unlike the Jews, the writer says, Christians have no country, language or customs of their own.
b: The contrast is with chapter 4: Jews were known by food, Sabbath and circumcision. Christians, the writer says, live in every city and look like their neighbors. What sets them apart is unseen (6:4). The passage that follows (5:1-6:10) is the most quoted part of the letter. The Catholic Encyclopedia sums it up: Christians 'are not of the world but citizens of heaven; yet they are the soul of the world'.

a: busybodies
p: Greek polypragmones, people busy with too many things. The same root as the Jews' 'fussing' at 4:6.
b: Polypragmōn is a meddler, a person with too many interests; the writer used the noun of the Jews at 4:6. Christian teaching, he says, is not the invention of restless thinkers, and Christians do not champion 'a human doctrine, as some are': a glance at the philosophical schools, whose views he mocks at 8:2.

a: in foreign ones
p: Greek barbaros: anyone who did not speak Greek.
b: Barbaros was the Greek word for a foreigner, someone whose speech sounded like 'bar-bar'. Paul is in debt 'both to Greeks and to barbarians' (Romans 1:14), and Colossians 3:11 says that in Christ there is no Greek or barbarian. The site renders it 'foreign' here so the word does not sound like 'savage'.

a: their own citizenship
p: Greek politeia: a city's constitution, and the life of its citizens.
b: Politeia is citizenship, the order of a city and the way its citizens live. The writer builds 5:4-10 on the word: Christians live in every city, but their own citizenship is ordered in a way no one expects. The verb comes at 5:9 ('they live as citizens of heaven') and 10:7. The site's Philippians 1:27 has the verb as 'live as citizens worthy of the good news of Christ'.

a: but as resident aliens
p: Greek paroikoi: foreigners who live in a city without its citizens' rights. 1 Peter's word for Christians.
b: A paroikos was a free foreigner living in a city that was not his, with a place there but no citizen's rights. The Greek Old Testament uses the word for Abraham in Canaan (Genesis 23:4, 'a foreigner living among you'); 1 Peter calls believers 'resident aliens and temporary residents' (1 Peter 2:11), and the letters of 1 Clement, Polycarp and the Martyrdom open with a church that 'lives as a resident alien' in its city (1 Clement 1:0). The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this verse, with 5:10 and 6:10, in its teaching on the duties of citizens: Christians 'reside in their own nations, but as resident aliens' (Catechism 2240, note 46).

a: Every foreign land is their homeland, and every homeland is a foreign land
p: The verse turns Hebrews 11's 'country in heaven' into a paradox.
b: Hebrews says the patriarchs 'admitted that they were foreigners and temporary residents on the earth' (Hebrews 11:13), because 'they are reaching for a better one, a country in heaven' (Hebrews 11:16). The writer draws both conclusions at once: since no earthly land is a Christian's true home, any land can be lived in as home, and none can be held as final. Jeremiah's letter to the exiles, 'Seek the peace of the city I sent you to' (Jeremiah 29:7), is the Old Testament form of the same balance.

a: their newborn children they do not throw away
t: They do not abandon their babies
p: Greek and Roman parents could leave an unwanted newborn to die. Christians, like Jews, would not.
b: Rhiptein is 'to throw out': the exposure of infants, leaving an unwanted baby outside to die or be taken by strangers. Justin Martyr told the emperor, 'we have been taught that to expose newly-born children is the part of wicked men', and that Christians fear to do it, 'lest some of them be not picked up, but die, and we become murderers' (First Apology 27 and 29, in the Ante-Nicene Fathers). The Didache says: 'You must not murder a child by abortion, and you must not kill one that has been born' (Didache 2:2).

a: They set out a shared table, but not a shared bed
p: 'Bed' is a scholar's guess that Lake prints. The manuscript repeats 'common'.
b: Lake's Greek is trapezan koinēn paratithentai, all' ou koitēn: 'a common table they set out, but not a bed'. The last word, koitēn 'bed', is not in the manuscript. Otto (1879) reports that the manuscript reads all' ou koinēn, 'but not a common one', and that koitēn was Maranus's conjecture, printed by Bunsen and Gildemeister; Otto kept the manuscript and took the second koinēn as 'unclean' (the sense of Acts 10:14): a shared table, but not an unclean one. Roberts and Donaldson's footnote says the same: 'Otto omits "bed," which is an emendation.' So the near-rhyme of koinēn and koitēn belongs to the conjecture, not to the manuscript; see the variant. On Lake's text, Christians are generous with food and hospitality but faithful in marriage; Lake gives the sense in other words: 'They offer free hospitality, but guard their purity.' On the manuscript's text, the point is that their meals are shared but clean.

a: They are in the flesh, but they do not live by the flesh
t: In the flesh, not by the flesh
p: Lake's margin: 2 Corinthians 10:3 and Romans 8:12-13.
b: Paul: 'We do live in the flesh. But we do not wage our war by the standards of the flesh' (2 Corinthians 10:3), and 'we do not owe it to the flesh, to live by the flesh' (Romans 8:12). 'Flesh' here is not the body as such but life run by human desires against God; the site renders sarx 'flesh' everywhere, as in Paul.

a: they live as citizens of heaven
p: Greek politeuontai, 'they are citizens'. Paul: 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven'.
b: Lake's margin points to Philippians 3:18-20, where Paul sets those whose 'thinking is on earthly things' against believers: 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven' (Philippians 3:20). Paul's noun is politeuma; the writer uses the verb from the same root. Philippi was a Roman colony whose people were citizens of a far-off Rome; the picture fitted them, and it fits the writer's Christians scattered through every city.

a: by the way they live they outdo the laws
t: Obeying the laws and going beyond them
p: Christians keep the city's laws and live better than the laws require.
b: The verb nikōsi is 'they conquer, they outdo'. The writer claims that Christians are law-abiding, which was the answer the apologists gave to charges of disloyalty, and more than law-abiding: they love their enemies (6:6) and do not abandon their children (5:6), though no Roman law required either. Paul teaches obedience to the authorities (Romans 13:1-7), and 1 Peter says, 'Submit yourselves to every authority that humans create, because of the Lord' (1 Peter 2:13); Jesus asks for a righteousness that overflows 'far beyond' that of the scribes (Matthew 5:20). Where obedience ends, the writer does not say; the site's cards at Romans 13 and Matthew 22 give how the churches answer. The Catechism cites this verse in its teaching on citizens' duties (2240).

a: No one knows them, and yet they are condemned
p: Lake's margin: 2 Corinthians 6:9-10. The writer builds 5:11-16 on Paul's list.
b: Paul described the apostles' life in contrasts: 'We are unknown, and yet recognized. We are dying, and look, we live on' (2 Corinthians 6:9). The writer takes the form and applies it to all Christians: unknown and condemned, killed and made alive. Being condemned without being known was the complaint the apologists made: Christians were punished for the name alone.

a: They are poor, and yet they make many rich
p: Word for word Paul's 2 Corinthians 6:10.
b: This is Paul's own line: 'We are poor, yet we make many rich' (2 Corinthians 6:10). The next clause rewords Paul's 'We own nothing, yet we hold everything' (2 Corinthians 6:10). Lake's margin marks both.

a: they are shown to be in the right
p: Greek dikaiountai, the verb of justification (9:4-5), here in its court sense.
b: Dikaioō is to declare someone in the right. Slandered by people, Christians are vindicated, whether by their lives or by God. The writer uses the same verb at 9:4-5 for God's justifying of sinners in his Son, so the reader can hear both senses.

a: They are insulted, and they bless
p: Lake's margin: 1 Corinthians 4:12.
b: Paul: 'When people insult us, we bless them' (1 Corinthians 4:12). Behind both stands Jesus' teaching to bless those who curse (Luke 6:28), and Paul's 'Bless your persecutors' (Romans 12:14).

a: as foreigners
p: Greek allophyloi. In the Greek Old Testament it is the word for the Philistines.
b: Allophylos means 'of another tribe or race'. The Greek Old Testament uses it again and again for the Philistines (for example 1 Samuel 17:1 in Swete's Septuagint). The writer says Jews fight Christians as outsiders, Greeks persecute them, and neither can give a reason. Hostility from Jewish communities is reported in Acts (Acts 13:50; Acts 14:19) and in the Martyrdom of Polycarp (13:1); the site's anti-Judaism page discusses how such reports were later used.
r: Acts 13:50; Acts 14:19; Martyrdom of Polycarp 13:1; 1 Thessalonians 2:14-15

a: what the soul is to a body
p: The letter's most famous image: Christians are to the world what the soul is to the body.
b: Chapter 6 works out one comparison in ten verses: the soul is spread through the body, unseen, at war with the flesh, shut up in it yet holding it together, immortal in a mortal tent. Lake prints the Greek hoper estin sōmati psychē, 'what the soul is to a body', without 'in', while the second half has 'in the world'. The image claims much: the world lives, in some sense, because of the Christians in it (6:7). It also pictures the soul as imprisoned in the body (6:7); see the note at 6:5 on how that fits the Bible.

a: they are not from the world
t: In the world, not from it
p: Lake's margin: John 17:11, 14, 16.
b: Jesus prayed for his disciples: 'They are not from the world, as I am not from the world' (John 17:16), and 'I am not asking you to remove them from the world' (John 17:15). The writer's comparison of soul and body is his way of saying the same thing.

a: kept under guard in the visible body
p: Greek phroureitai, 'kept by a garrison'. The same root as 'prison' in 6:7.
b: Phroureō is to keep under guard, as a garrison keeps a town; phroura in 6:7 is a guard post or prison. The soul is held in the body as Christians are held in the world. Christians are seen, but 'their reverence for God stays out of sight': the inner life of faith cannot be shown to an outsider, which is why 4:6 said it cannot be learned from a human being.

a: The flesh hates the soul and makes war on it
t: Compared with the Bible: soul and flesh
p: Here 'flesh' is close to 'body'. In Paul the war is between the flesh and God's Spirit.
b: Matches: 1 Peter speaks of the flesh's desires, which 'are at war with the soul' (1 Peter 2:11), and Lake's margin gives Galatians 5:17 ('The flesh desires what is against the Spirit'). Goes beyond: the writer's comparison makes the body itself the soul's jailer (6:7), a picture closer to Greek philosophy than to Genesis, where God forms the human body and calls his work 'very good' (Genesis 1:31; Genesis 2:7), or to Paul, who looks for the body's resurrection, not escape from it (1 Corinthians 15:42-44). The writer does not deny the resurrection; he simply does not speak of it.

a: Christians love those who hate them
p: Lake's margin: Matthew 5:44 and Luke 6:27.
b: 'Keep loving your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you' (Matthew 5:44); 'Treat well the people who hate you' (Luke 6:27). The soul loves even the body that fights it; Christians love even the world that hates them.

a: they are the ones who hold the world together
p: Lake compares Aristides: the world stands through the Christians' prayers.
b: Lake's note: 'Cf. Aristides, Apology 16. ‘I have no doubt but that the world stands through the intercession of Christians.’' The Ante-Nicene Fathers' English of the same chapter, as revised at New Advent, reads: 'to me there is no doubt but that the earth abides through the supplication of the Christians.' The thought has a biblical root in Abraham's plea that God would spare Sodom for the sake of ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32), and in Jesus' words that his disciples are 'the salt of the earth' (Matthew 5:13).

a: a mortal tent
p: Greek skēnōma, 'tent', a picture of the body Paul and 2 Peter use.
b: Paul calls the body 'the earthly house we live in, this tent' (2 Corinthians 5:1), and Peter speaks of being 'still in this tent' (2 Peter 1:13). The soul is immortal; the tent is not. Christians, likewise, 'live as resident aliens' (paroikousin, the verb of 5:5) among perishable things and wait for 'the incorruption that is in heaven' (aphtharsia, the site's 'incorruption').

a: stationed them at a post
t: A post they may not leave
p: Greek taxis, a soldier's place in the line. Lake: the church as God's army.
b: Taxis is order, rank, a soldier's assigned station. Lake's note: 'There is probably a recurrence of the idea of the church as the ‘militia dei’' (the army of God), with a cross-reference to his note on the Shepherd of Hermas. The writer has just said that persecution makes Christians grow (6:9); God has placed them at their post, and they are not allowed to beg off. The Catechism of the Catholic Church cites this verse with 5:5 and 5:10 (2240).

a: a plan of merely human mysteries
p: Lake's margin: 1 Corinthians 9:17, 'trusted with a stewardship'.
b: The Greek oikonomian ... pepisteuntai is close to Paul's 'I have still been trusted with a stewardship' (1 Corinthians 9:17), the same noun and verb. The writer says that what Christians guard is not a human secret. His contrast may glance at the Greek 'mysteries', the secret rites of initiation in cults of his day; he does not name them.

a: the holy Word
p: Greek logos, as in John 1:1. The writer never uses the name Jesus or Christ.
b: God himself 'set the truth and the holy Word ... among people'. The Logos is the one through whom God made the heavens, the one he sent (7:2), whom the next verses call his Son (7:4). John: 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). Remarkably, the letter never names Jesus or Christ: it speaks of the Word, the Son, the servant and the Savior (9:6). To a pagan reader, logos was also the Greek name for the reason that orders the world, so the word met him on his own ground.
orig: τὸν λόγον τὸν ἅγιον (ton logon ton hagion)

a: He sent the very Craftsman and Creator of the universe himself
t: Not an attendant or an angel, but the Creator
p: The writer says God sent not an angel or ruler but the one through whom he made everything.
b: This is the heart of the writer's answer. God did not send 'some attendant, or an angel, or a ruler', but the Craftsman (technitēs) and Creator (dēmiourgos) of all. The New Testament says the same of the Son: 'Through him everything came to exist' (John 1:3); 'in him all things were created' (Colossians 1:16); 'through him he also made the ages' (Hebrews 1:2). The Wisdom of Solomon uses technitēs of God himself: people 'did not recognize the Craftsman' (Wisdom of Solomon 13:1). Here the title is given to the one God sent. The Son is not one of God's creatures but the one by whom they were made. The word for 'attendant', hypēretēs, is an aide who carries out another's orders. It is not the word the letter uses for the Son at 8:9-9:1 (pais, 'Child'): see the note at 8:9.
r: John 1:3; Colossians 1:15-17; Hebrews 1:2-3; Hebrews 1:14; Wisdom of Solomon 13:1

a: By him he shut the sea within its own bounds
t: The sea kept within its bounds
p: The Old Testament's picture of the Creator setting limits for the sea.
b: God asks Job, 'Who closed doors to hold back the sea' (Job 38:8); Proverbs tells of the time 'when he laid down for the sea its fixed line' (Proverbs 8:29); Jeremiah: 'I made the sand a border for the sea' (Jeremiah 5:22). The writer gives these works of God to the Word.

a: The moon obeys him when he commands it to shine at night
t: Sun, moon and stars obey him
p: The heavens keep the Word's order. A contrast with the Jews' moon-watching at 4:5.
b: The sun keeps the 'measures of the day's courses', the moon shines at his command, and the stars follow the moon's course, as ancient astronomy saw them moving across the sky with it. Psalm 104 says God 'made the moon to keep the appointed times' (Psalm 104:19). Earlier the writer scorned those who 'keep close watch on the stars and the moon' to fix feasts (4:5); here he turns to the moon as a servant of the Word.

a: All the elements faithfully keep his mysteries
p: Greek stoicheia, the basic stuffs of the world: here fire, air, earth and water.
b: Stoicheia were the 'elements' of Greek science. The list at the end of the verse, 'fire, air, the abyss', runs through them. At 8:2 the writer mocks philosophers who made God one of 'the elements that God created'. Paul uses stoicheia in another sense, of the 'weak and poor elements' that once enslaved the Galatians (Galatians 4:9).

a: As a king sends his son, he sent him as a king
p: The Greek can be read 'as a king sends his son who is a king'. Either way the Son is royal.
b: Hōs basileus pempōn huion basilea epempsen: 'as a king sending a son king he sent'. The second 'king' can go with 'son' (a son who is himself a king) or with 'he sent' (he sent him as king). Lake: 'as a king sending a son, he sent him as King'. Lake's margin at 7:3 points to Zechariah 9:9: 'Look, your king is coming to you', the gentle king on a donkey.
orig: ὡς βασιλεὺς πέμπων υἱὸν βασιλέα ἔπεμψεν

a: He sent him as God. He sent him as a human being to human beings
t: Sent as God and as man
p: An early statement that the one sent was both God and human.
b: The writer says, in two short clauses, that the Son came 'as God' and 'as a human being to human beings'. He does not explain how; the later creeds and councils took up that question. The New Testament says that 'the Word became flesh' (John 1:14) and that 'the Word was God' (John 1:1). The homily of chapter 11 adds that the Word 'appeared as new' and is 'born young in the hearts of the saints' (11:4).

a: For force has no place in God
p: Lake: 'for compulsion is not an attribute of God'.
b: Bia gar ou proseiti tō theō: force does not belong to God. Lake renders 'for compulsion is not an attribute of God'. The writer sets persuasion against tyranny, fear and terror (7:3). He writes as one of a persecuted minority. Whether rulers may use force for true religion became a later question; the site's card at 1 Kings 18 gives how the churches answer it.
orig: βία γὰρ οὐ πρόσεστι τῷ θεῷ

a: He sent him in love, not in judgment
p: Lake's margin: John 3:17.
b: 'For God sent the Son into the world, not to pass judgment on the world, but so that through him the world would be saved' (John 3:17). The writer's next line (7:6) keeps the other half of the New Testament's teaching: one day he will send him to judge.

a: who will remain standing at his coming
p: Lake's margin: Malachi 3:2. The Greek verb is the Septuagint's.
b: Malachi asks, 'Who can remain standing when he appears?' (Malachi 3:2). The writer's verb, hypostēsetai, is the one the Greek of Malachi 3:2 uses, and he joins it to parousia, 'coming', the New Testament's word for Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 4:15). The first coming was in gentleness (7:4); the second will be in judgment. Here the manuscript breaks off: see the variant on '...'.

a: thrown to wild beasts
p: The text resumes in the middle of a sentence about the martyrs.
b: After the gap, the sentence begins with a participle: '... thrown to wild beasts to make them deny the Lord, and not overcome?' Lake suggests that 'Do you not see that' stood before it, and the Plain English Translation supplies those words in brackets (see the variant). Death by wild beasts in the arena was a Roman punishment that Christians met: Ignatius expected it (Ignatius to the Romans 4:1), and the proconsul threatened Polycarp with it (Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:1). The writer offers the martyrs' endurance as evidence: no human power explains it (7:9).
r: 7:9; Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:1; Ignatius to the Romans 4:1; Hebrews 11:33

a: others growing in number
p: The writer argues that punishment only makes the church grow.
b: The writer has already said that Christians, 'when they are punished day after day, grow all the more in number' (6:9). Acts tells a like story: after Stephen's death the scattered believers 'went from place to place, telling the good news of the word' (Acts 8:4). The growth is, for the writer, one of the 'proofs' of 7:9.

a: These are the proofs of his coming
p: Greek parousia: 'presence' or 'arrival'. Here it is Christ's coming already shown in the martyrs' strength.
b: Parousia means presence, arrival. At 7:6 the word was the coming in judgment. Here the martyrs' courage and the church's growth are 'proofs of his coming': most naturally, evidence that he has come and is at work, though the sentence could also mean signs of the coming still ahead. The writer's other word for the evidence, dynamis theou, 'the power of God', is Paul's phrase for the message of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18).

a: who among human beings knew at all what God is
t: Compared with the Bible: knowing God before Christ
p: The writer says no one knew God before Christ came. Paul and Justin allowed more.
b: Matches: 'Nobody has ever seen God' (John 1:18), and only the Son makes him known. Goes beyond: Paul says God's 'unseen qualities ... are visible to the mind in what he has made' (Romans 1:20), and that he 'did not leave himself without a witness' (Acts 14:17); the psalms say the heavens tell of God (Psalm 19:1). Justin Martyr went further the other way and said that 'those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists', naming Socrates and Heraclitus (First Apology 46). The writer, writing against the philosophers, allows no such knowledge: before Christ came, people did not know God (8:1, 5). The site's page on knowing God from creation gives the churches' views.

a: Some of them said God is fire
p: The Greek thinkers who made one element the source of all things.
b: From the earliest Greek philosophers on, thinkers sought one first stuff behind everything: water for Thales, fire for Heraclitus; the Stoics taught that God is a fiery reason that runs through the world. The writer lumps them together and mocks them. The Wisdom of Solomon, a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, makes the same complaint against those who 'took fire, or wind, or quick-moving air' for gods (Wisdom of Solomon 13:2). The site's Acts 17:18 shows Paul debating 'Epicurean and Stoic philosophers' in Athens.

a: they call God the very thing they are about to go into!
t: The fire they will go into
p: A jab with two possible targets: the Stoic end of the world in fire, or the fire of judgment.
b: The aside can be read in two ways. Read with the philosophers, it may point to the Stoic teaching that the world will at last be taken up into fire: those who call God fire are calling God the thing that will swallow them. Read with the writer's own warnings, it may be a threat: they make a god of the fire into which they will be cast, the 'eternal fire' of 10:7. The Greek allows both.

a: sorcerers
p: Greek goētes: wizards, charlatans. A hard word for philosophers.
b: A goēs was a sorcerer or a quack, someone who fools people with tricks. Teratia, the word before it, is talk of marvels, wonder-mongering. To call the 'trustworthy' philosophers (8:2) sorcerers is the writer's sharpest insult.

a: But he has shown himself
p: No one has seen God. He has made himself known.
b: 'Nobody has ever seen God. It is the only one, God, the one in the Father's embrace, who has made him known' (John 1:18). 1 Timothy says of God: 'No human being has seen him, and none can see him' (1 Timothy 6:16). The writer agrees and adds how God has shown himself: 'through faith' (8:6).

a: the only way anyone is allowed to see God
p: Faith is the eye that sees God.
b: 'Without faith no one can please him at all' (Hebrews 11:6). Hebrews 11:27 says Moses held out as one who saw the unseen God. The writer has said that Christians' reverence for God is invisible (6:4); now he says what sees the invisible.

a: a lover of humankind
p: Greek philanthrōpos, the word behind 'philanthropy'.
b: Philanthrōpos was a quality praised in kings and gods. Titus speaks of 'the kindness of God our Savior and his love for humankind' (Titus 3:4), and the writer uses the noun at 9:2. Lake's margin at 9:1-2 points to Titus 3:3-5: the writer's story of God's patience follows Titus's pattern of 'once we were ... but when the kindness of God appeared'.

a: free from anger
t: Compared with the Bible: a God without anger?
p: The writer calls God 'free from anger'. The Bible speaks often of God's anger.
b: Aorgētos means 'free from anger', not merely 'slow to anger' (that is makrothymos, 'patient', in 8:7). Matches: God is 'slow to anger, great in loyal love' (Exodus 34:6) and kind to the ungrateful (Luke 6:35). Goes beyond, and is in tension: the Bible speaks plainly of God's anger: 'God's anger is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of people' (Romans 1:18). The writer himself speaks of the eternal fire for the condemned (10:7), so he does not deny judgment; his word stresses that God is never moved by passion, as human anger is.

a: he alone is good
p: Mark 10:18.
b: Jesus said, 'No one is good except one: God' (Mark 10:18). The writer piles up the words for God's goodness, 'kind and good and free from anger and true', and ends with Jesus' saying.

a: his Child alone
p: Greek pais means 'child' and also 'servant'. Here the Plain English Translation has 'Child', as Lake does.
b: Pais stands here and at 8:11 and 9:1. It means a child, and also a servant: the Greek of Isaiah 42:1 calls God's chosen one ho pais mou, and Matthew quotes it of Jesus: 'Look: my servant, whom I chose, / my beloved' (Matthew 12:18); Acts uses it of Jesus too: 'the God of our ancestors, who has given glory to his servant Jesus' (Acts 3:13). The site keeps 'servant' for pais of Jesus in the other early Christian writings. Here it has 'Child', as Lake does, for two reasons. The letter has just said that God did not send 'some attendant' (7:2, a different word, hypēretēs), so 'servant' here would seem to take that back. And the letter calls him 'Son' (huios) before and after (7:4; 9:2; 9:4; 10:2), so 'Child' is the plain sense of a Father who shares his thought with his own. Roberts and Donaldson translate 'Son'.

a: in a mystery
p: God's plan kept secret for ages, then shown.
b: Paul speaks of 'the unveiling of the mystery kept in silence for long ages' (Romans 16:25) and 'the mystery that was kept hidden from the ages' (Colossians 1:26). The writer adds a pastoral point: while God kept his plan hidden, 'he seemed to neglect us and not to care'. That answers Diognetus's question why the faith came so late (1:1).

a: what had been prepared from the beginning
p: The gifts God planned before the world.
b: Paul: 'all that God has prepared for those who love him' (1 Corinthians 2:9). Matthew 25:34 speaks of a kingdom made ready from the world's foundation. The writer's question 'Which of us would ever have expected these things?' returns in 9:5: 'the good gifts no one expected'.

a: up to the former time he let us be swept along
t: God's patience in the former time
p: Lake's margin: Romans 3:21-26 and Titus 3:3.
b: Paul says that God 'in his forbearance ... had passed over sins done earlier' (Romans 3:25), and in Athens that 'God has looked past those times of not knowing' (Acts 17:30). Titus describes the old life: 'slaves to desires and pleasures of every kind' (Titus 3:3). The writer gives a reason for the waiting: God let people prove by their own deeds that they could not reach life, so that the gift would be seen as a gift.

a: enter the kingdom of God
p: Lake's margin: John 3:5.
b: Jesus told Nicodemus, 'unless someone is born from water and Spirit, he has no way to enter the kingdom of God' (John 3:5). The writer's point is the same: what is impossible for us is made possible 'by God's power'.

a: its wages, punishment and death
p: Romans 6:23, in other Greek words.
b: Paul: 'Sin pays wages, and the wages are death' (Romans 6:23). The writer uses another word for wages (misthos, where Paul has opsōnia) and adds 'punishment'. Our wrongdoing had to come 'to its full measure' first, as the Amorites' had to before Israel's conquest (Genesis 15:16).

a: a ransom on our behalf
p: Greek lytron, the price paid to free a captive or slave. Lake's margin: 1 Timothy 2:6.
b: God 'handed over his own Son, a ransom on our behalf'. Jesus came 'to give his life as a ransom in place of many' (Mark 10:45), and 1 Timothy says, 'He gave himself as a ransom on behalf of all' (1 Timothy 2:6). Lake's margin adds Romans 8:32 ('He did not hold back his own Son. He handed him over for us all') and Ephesians 1:7. The writer does not say to whom the ransom was paid; neither does the New Testament.

a: the righteous for the unrighteous
p: 1 Peter 3:18 in the same Greek words, which Lake's margin gives.
b: 1 Peter: Christ suffered 'the one who was righteous for those who were not' (1 Peter 3:18); the Greek of both is dikaios hyper adikōn. The writer builds a chain of five contrasts on it: holy and lawless, blameless and wicked, righteous and unrighteous, incorruptible and corruptible, immortal and mortal.

a: cover our sins
p: The Psalms' picture of forgiveness.
b: 'Happy is the one whose rebellion is lifted away, / whose sin is covered over' (Psalm 32:1), which Paul quotes in Romans 4:7. The writer says what covers them: not sacrifice (3:5), but 'his righteousness', the Son's.

a: Oh, the sweet exchange!
p: What the 'exchange' is, in the writer's own words.
b: Antallagē is an exchange, one thing given in place of another. The lines say what the exchange is: the lawlessness of many hidden in one righteous man, the righteousness of one making many lawless people righteous. The thought is Paul's: 'God made the one who did not know sin to be sin for us, so that in him we could become the righteousness of God' (2 Corinthians 5:21). The writer gives no theory beyond the exchange itself. The site's cards at 2 Corinthians 5 ('How does the cross save?'), Romans 3 and 1 John 2 set out the churches' answers with their sources.

a: the workmanship no one can trace out
p: Greek anexichniastos, 'with no tracks to follow', as in Romans 11:33 and Ephesians 3:8.
b: Paul uses the word of God's ways, which no one can 'follow the tracks' of (Romans 11:33), and of 'riches no one can trace out' (Ephesians 3:8). Dēmiourgia, 'workmanship', is the word of making and creating: the writer calls the cross a work of the Creator (7:2).

a: the righteousness of one should justify many who are lawless
p: Romans 5 and Isaiah 53.
b: Paul: 'the one man obeyed, and the many will be made righteous' (Romans 5:19); Isaiah's servant: 'By his knowledge my servant, the righteous one, will put the many in the right' (Isaiah 53:11). The writer's 'justify' (dikaiōsē) is the verb of 9:4 and of Paul's teaching on justification.

a: doctor
p: Eleven names for what God is to us, from 'the one who raises us' to 'life'.
b: The list runs: tropheus (one who rears a child), father, teacher, counselor, iatros (doctor, the site's word, as in Mark 2:17), mind, light, honor, glory, strength, life. The writer then quotes the sense of Jesus' words, not to worry about clothing and food: 'So stop worrying' (Matthew 6:31), which Lake's margin gives. It is not clear whether the names belong to the Father or to the Savior just named; the Greek auton, 'him', could be either.

a: full knowledge of the Father
p: Greek epignōsis. Here the sentence may break off: Lake marks a gap; Otto read it as complete.
b: Epignōsis is knowledge that recognizes and grasps, the New Testament's word in Colossians 1:9-10. In Lake's text 'first of all' (prōton men) expects a 'then' that never comes, and Lake marks a gap ('Here again there is apparently a lacuna in the text'). Otto (1879) read the sentence as complete, 'If you long for this faith, you will also receive first of all knowledge of the Father', and found the answering 'then' at 10:3 ('And once you know him'). Roberts and Donaldson follow that reading. See the variant on '...'.

a: For God loved human beings
p: Lake's margin: John 3:16 and 1 John 4:9.
b: 'For this is how God loved the world: he gave his only Son' (John 3:16). 1 John: 'God has sent his only Son into the world so that we may live through him' (1 John 4:9). The verse is a list of God's gifts to humans, each beginning 'to them' or 'them', and ending with the gift still to come.

a: Them he formed from his own image
p: Genesis 1:26-27 (Lake's margin).
b: Genesis: 'So God created the human in his image' (Genesis 1:27). The writer says 'from' (ek) his image, and 'formed' (eplase), the verb the Greek Genesis uses for the forming of Adam from the dust (Genesis 2:7). The gifts of reason and mind and the freedom to 'look up' to God belong with the image.

a: the one who loved you first like this
p: 1 John 4:19, Lake's margin.
b: 'We love because he loved us first' (1 John 4:19). The writer turns it into a question to Diognetus: once you know such a God, how could you not love him?

a: an imitator of his kindness
p: Greek mimētēs, 'imitator', as in Ephesians 5:1.
b: Paul: 'become imitators of God, like children who are loved' (Ephesians 5:1). Jesus: 'Become compassionate, the way your Father is compassionate' (Luke 6:36). The writer says what imitation means: not power over others (10:5) but carrying their burdens and giving (10:6). Justin, too, joins the thought that God needs no offerings with the thought that he accepts those who imitate his goodness (First Apology 10).

a: when God wills
p: Greek thelontos autou, 'he willing': God's will, or the person's?
b: The phrase is short and could mean 'when God wills it' or 'if he (the person) is willing'. The Plain English Translation takes it of God, because the subject of the sentence is the human being and a separate 'he' most naturally points back to God. Lake keeps it open: 'it is possible when he will'.

a: ruling your neighbors by force
p: Happiness is not in domination, greed or wealth.
b: The writer lists the marks of power as the world prized it: domination over neighbors, having more than the weak, wealth used to push others around. None of these imitates God, who 'sent him to save and to persuade, not to force' (7:4). Jesus said the same to his disciples about the rulers of the nations (Mark 10:42-45).

a: becomes a god to those who receive it
p: The boldest phrase in the letter. The giver acts toward the needy as God acts.
b: The Greek says plainly that the generous person 'becomes a god (theos) of those who receive'. The Plain English Translation keeps the lowercase 'a god' and the boldness. In context the sense is that God is the great giver, and whoever passes on God's gifts to the needy stands to them in God's place. It is the culmination of 'imitator of God' (10:4-6), not a claim that the giver becomes divine by nature; the site's cards at Psalm 82 and 2 Peter 1, which ask whether people can share God's nature, take up a different question. Lake's margin gives Galatians 6:2 ('Carry each other's heavy loads') and Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1, where masters are reminded that they have a Master in heaven.

a: God governs in heaven
p: Greek politeuetai, the verb of 5:9 ('live as citizens'), now used of God.
b: The verb politeuomai means to live as a citizen, and also to govern a city's affairs. At 5:9 Christians 'live as citizens of heaven'; here the subject is God. Lake keeps the first sense ('God lives in heaven'); Roberts and Donaldson take the second ('rules'), and so does the Plain English Translation, since God is not a citizen of his city but the one who runs it. Either way the repetition is the point: the citizenship Christians hold is in God's own city.

a: the eternal fire
p: The Gospels' phrase for final punishment.
b: Jesus spoke of 'the eternal fire made ready for the devil and his angels' (Matthew 25:41), and Jude of Sodom's 'punishment of eternal fire' (Jude 7). The writer sets 'what passes for death here' against 'the real death' kept for the condemned (Matthew 10:28; Revelation 20:14). The Martyrdom of Polycarp has the same contrast between a fire 'that burns for an hour' and 'the fire of the coming judgment' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:2).
r: Matthew 25:41; Jude 7; Matthew 10:28; Revelation 20:14; Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:2

a: which will punish to the end those handed over to it
p: Greek mechri telous: 'to the very end' or 'until an end'. The phrase bears on how long punishment lasts.
b: Mechri telous usually means 'to the end, completely' (as Hebrews 3:14). Read so, the fire punishes those handed over to it completely, without letup; the contrast with 'the fire that lasts a short time' (10:8) suggests that the writer thinks of it as lasting. A reader could also hear 'until the end', as if the punishment has a limit. The Greek alone does not settle the question that the site's pages on the final judgment and Gehenna take up.

a: the fire that lasts a short time
p: Christians were burned alive. The writer sets that fire against 'that other fire'.
b: To pyr to proskairon, the fire 'for a season', is Lake's text, and it means the fire of execution. Otto (1879) reports that it was his own earlier conjecture, which later editors followed, and that Reuss, reading the manuscript for him, found 'this fire' (to pyr touto) and no room for proskairon; see the variant. Either way this fire is set against 'that other fire'. Polycarp, threatened with burning, answered: 'You threaten a fire that burns for an hour and is soon put out' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:2). Here the letter, as it survives, ends. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that 'the letter breaks off at the end of chapter x; it may have originally been much longer'. Lake marks no gap here, but Otto reports a note in the manuscript's margin where 11:1 begins: kai hōde enkopēn eiche to antigraphon, 'here too the copy had a break'.
r: Martyrdom of Polycarp 11:2; Martyrdom of Polycarp 2:3; Daniel 3:17-18; 1 Peter 4:12

a: I became a disciple of apostles
p: Lake: chapters 11-12 'belong to a different document', probably a homily, perhaps by Hippolytus.
b: Lake: 'The concluding chapters (xi-xii) have clearly no connection with the preceding ones, and it is generally conceded that they belong to a different document, probably an Epiphany homily, though possibly, as Otto thought, an Easter homily. Bonwetsch has shown very strong reasons for thinking that Hippolytus was the author.' The Catholic Encyclopedia agrees that they 'bear no relation to the rest of the letter' and 'seem to be a fragment of a homily of later date'. It adds that 'through a misunderstanding' of the words 'disciple of the Apostles' the letter has 'since the eighteenth century' been classed among the Apostolic Fathers. The English of the Ante-Nicene Fathers titles the whole work 'The Epistle of Mathetes to Diognetus': mathētēs is the Greek word for 'disciple' in this verse, made into a name.

a: a teacher of the nations
p: Greek ethnē, 'nations', the Gentiles. Paul's title in 1 Timothy 2:7.
b: The preacher calls himself 'a teacher of the nations', Paul's description of himself: 'I was made a teacher of the Gentiles' (1 Timothy 2:7). Ethnē is the word for the non-Jewish peoples (Lake: 'the heathen'). In 11:3 the nations are set against 'the people', Israel.

a: has come to love the Word
p: The homily speaks of the Word (logos) in almost every verse.
b: In 11:2-12:9 logos comes again and again: the Word appeared, spoke boldly, was sent, is born in the saints, commands the preacher and teaches the saints. The site renders it 'the Word' where it names the Son and 'word' at 12:7, where it may mean the message. Lake's margin at 11:2 points to John 1:9: 'The real light, which shines on every person, was on its way into the world.'

a: The people dishonored him
p: Lake: laos is 'the chosen people of Israel, in contrast with ta ethnē, the heathen nations'.
b: Lake's note: 'laos is here, as frequently, the chosen people of Israel, in contrast with ta ethnē, the heathen nations.' The three clauses echo 1 Timothy 3:16, which Lake's margin gives, where Christ was 'heralded among the nations', and John: 'his own people did not welcome him' (John 1:11). Unlike chapters 3-4, the homily says nothing more against the Jews.

a: He is the one from the beginning
p: Lake's margin: 1 John 1:1.
b: 'What was from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes' (1 John 1:1). The preacher answers the charge of newness that Diognetus raised (1:1): the Word 'appeared as new' but 'was discovered to be old'. He is also 'born young in the hearts of the saints', a picture of Christ formed in believers (Galatians 4:19).

a: who today is reckoned as Son
p: Lake: the 'today' suggests a homily for the Nativity, kept with the Epiphany.
b: 'Today' recalls Psalm 2:7, 'This day I have fathered you', and the voice at Jesus' baptism (Matthew 3:17), both in Lake's margin. Lake's note: 'This suggests that the homily belongs to a feast of the Nativity. In the time of Hippolytus this was probably not separated from the Epiphany or feast of the Baptism (see article on Christmas in Hastings Dictionary of Religion and Ethics.)'

a: move the boundary stones of the fathers
p: Proverbs 22:28.
b: 'Do not shift the old boundary line / that your ancestors laid down' (Proverbs 22:28). The preacher applies it to the faith: grace is given to those who keep 'the pledges of faith' and do not move the limits set by 'the fathers', the teachers who came before.

a: the fear of the Law is sung
p: A sequence of the Scriptures and the church's tradition.
b: The verse names the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels (plural) and the apostles' tradition, then the church. It is a witness, from the homily's own time, to Christians reading the Gospels beside the Law and the Prophets. The verb is aidō, 'sing'.

a: If you do not grieve this grace
p: Ephesians 4:30.
b: 'And do not cause grief to the Holy Spirit of God' (Ephesians 4:30). The homily speaks of 'grace' where Paul speaks of the Spirit: the grace of 11:5-6 that gives understanding and reveals mysteries.

a: a paradise of delight
p: The Greek Genesis's name for Eden. Those who love God become a new Eden.
b: Paradeisos tryphēs is the Septuagint's phrase for the garden of Eden (Genesis 3:23-24 in Swete's text; the site's Genesis, from the Hebrew, has 'the garden of Eden'). Lake's margin gives Genesis 2:15 and 3:24. The preacher reads the garden as a picture of the believer: those who love God rightly become the garden, and the tree grows in them.

a: a tree of knowledge
p: Greek gnōsis. Not yet the 'knowledge' of later Gnostic groups.
b: Genesis calls it 'the tree of knowing good and evil' (Genesis 2:9); the homily calls it simply the tree of knowledge (gnōsis). The site renders gnōsis 'knowledge' in all the early Christian writings, never 'gnosis', because the word is not yet the name of the secret knowledge that later Gnostic teachers claimed. The preacher does insist that knowledge must go with life and love (12:4-6).

a: disobedience kills
t: Compared with the Bible: the two trees
p: The homily says the tree of knowledge was good and only disobedience killed.
b: Matches: in Genesis the sin is disobedience to God's command (Genesis 2:17; Genesis 3:11), and Paul: 'One man disobeyed, and the many were made sinners' (Romans 5:19). Goes beyond: Genesis forbids the tree of knowledge (Genesis 2:17) and keeps the way to the tree of life guarded (Genesis 3:24); the homily reads the two trees as meant to go together, knowledge leading to life (12:3-4), so that the first people's fault was to use knowledge 'not purely'. That is a reading of Genesis, not something Genesis says.

a: they were stripped bare by the snake's deceit
p: Genesis 3:7 and 3:13.
b: After they ate, 'they realized they were naked' (Genesis 3:7), and Eve said, 'The snake fooled me, and I ate' (Genesis 3:13). Paul: 'the snake fooled Eve with his cunning' (2 Corinthians 11:3). The homily's 'stripped bare' (gegymnōntai) makes the nakedness a loss, as though the first people had been clothed with life before.

a: Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up
p: 'The apostle says': 1 Corinthians 8:1, word for word.
b: This is the only Scripture quoted with a formula in Diognetus 1-12: 'the apostle ... says'. The Greek is exactly Paul's, and the site's wording of 1 Corinthians 8:1 is used: 'Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.' In Paul it answers Corinthians who knew idols were nothing and ate food offered to them without care for weaker believers. The preacher uses it for knowledge cut off from 'the truth of the command that leads to life'.

a: whoever thinks he knows anything
p: 1 Corinthians 8:2, the next verse in Paul.
b: Paul goes on: 'If anyone thinks he has come to know something, he has not yet known it the way it must be known' (1 Corinthians 8:2). The preacher continues with Paul's verse in his own words and adds the snake: such a person is 'led astray by the snake'.

a: plants in hope, expecting fruit
p: Lake's margin: 1 Corinthians 9:10.
b: Paul: 'The one who plows should plow in hope' (1 Corinthians 9:10). The preacher keeps the garden picture of 12:1: true knowledge, joined to fear of God and the search for life, is a planting that will bear fruit.

a: given room in you
p: Greek chōroumenos: 'contained', 'made room for', 'grasped'.
b: The line is very compressed: 'Let your heart be knowledge, and life the true word, being contained.' Chōreō means to make room for, to hold, and so to take in or grasp. Lake: 'your life the true and comprehended word'. The Plain English Translation reads it as the word welcomed and held within. Whether logos here is the Word himself or the true message is open; the site writes 'word'.

a: And Eve is not corrupted, but a virgin is trusted
p: An early pairing of Eve and Mary, or a picture of the believer kept pure.
b: Eve was deceived by the snake; 'a virgin is trusted' (or 'believed', pisteuetai). Justin Martyr had already set the two side by side: 'For Eve, who was a virgin and undefiled, having conceived the word of the serpent, brought forth disobedience and death', 'But the Virgin Mary received faith and joy' (Dialogue with Trypho 100). Read that way, the homily points to Mary, who believed (Luke 1:38; Luke 1:45). It can also be read of the soul or the church as a virgin kept for Christ, as Paul writes: 'so that I could present you to Christ as a pure virgin' (2 Corinthians 11:2), where the next verse names Eve.

a: the Lord's Passover goes forward
p: The Christian Pascha. Lake reports Otto's view that the homily was for Easter.
b: To kyriou pascha is the Passover of the Lord, the Christian feast of Christ's death and resurrection (Pascha, Easter). Lake reports that Otto thought chapters 11-12 'an Easter homily', while Lake himself took the 'today' of 11:5 to point to the Nativity and Epiphany. 'The seasons are brought together' is Lake's text, from Sylburg's conjecture; the manuscript reads kēroi, 'candles', which Otto (1879) kept and took for the candles of the Easter night (see the variant). Read as 'seasons', the words may speak of the church's year of feasts; the homily does not say more.

a: To him be the glory forever. Amen.
p: The Greek 'to whom' can point to the Father or to the Word.
b: The doxology hō hē doxa eis tous aiōnas follows 'through him the Father is glorified'. 'To whom' most naturally refers to the Word, the subject of the sentence, but it could be the Father. New Testament doxologies are given both to God (Romans 16:27) and to Christ (2 Peter 3:18).
